Couples & Marriage

5 Myths About Couples Therapy That Stop Delhi Couples From Seeking Help

Is counselling only for couples about to divorce? Will the therapist take sides? Honest answers to the beliefs that cause most of the delay.

Home / Blog / 5 Myths About Couples Therapy
Reviewed by Dr. Supriya Malik Founder, eMbrace. 17+ years in psychology and developmental care.
Published 28 August 2026

You have talked about it. Perhaps one of you has looked up a number and not called it. Something has been off for a while, not dramatic, just tiring, and the idea of sitting in a room with a stranger to discuss your marriage feels like more than you want to take on.

Couples rarely delay because things are fine. They delay because of what they assume counselling will involve. Five beliefs cause most of that delay, and all five are worth examining before you decide.

Why so many Delhi couples wait years before booking

Marriage counselling in Delhi carries a particular weight. In the Indian context, marriage is not only a private relationship between two people, it is a social institution shaped by family expectations, tradition and community. That makes marital difficulty harder to name openly, and much harder to take outside the house.

Research on family therapy in India describes exactly this pattern: help-seeking for marital problems is stigmatised, to the point that families often present for some other reason rather than naming the marriage as the difficulty. There is also a real fear that seeking help outside the family somehow weakens it.

None of that makes the difficulty smaller. It just means it stays private for longer, and the patterns get more established while it does.

Myth 1
Counselling is only for couples about to divorce

This is the most common reason people wait, and it has the logic backwards. By the time a relationship is genuinely at the point of ending, counselling has the least to work with.

The couples who benefit most are frequently not in crisis at all. They are the ones noticing that the same argument keeps returning, that conversations have become logistics, or that they have quietly stopped raising things because it does not seem worth the friction. Those patterns are far easier to shift before they harden.

Counselling is also not only for marriages. Engaged couples, long-term partners and couples approaching a big transition use it too, which is why pre-marital counselling exists as a distinct service rather than a version of crisis repair.

Myth 2
The therapist will take sides

Almost everyone arrives half expecting to be judged, and often quietly hoping the therapist will confirm they were right. Neither happens.

In couples work, the client is the relationship rather than either individual. A trained couples therapist is not there to decide who was correct about the incident last month. They are there to make the pattern underneath it visible to both of you, which is usually more useful and considerably less comfortable than a verdict.

In practice, neutrality is active work. It looks like both partners getting equal room to speak, neither being allowed to dominate the session, and the therapist interrupting a familiar loop rather than letting it play out as it does at home.

Myth 3
Our problems should stay inside the family

This is the belief the research describes most directly, and it deserves a straight answer rather than reassurance.

Counselling sessions are confidential. What is discussed is not shared with parents, in-laws, extended family or anyone else without your consent. The narrow exceptions are legal ones, where there is serious risk of harm. Speaking to a qualified clinician is not the same as the matter becoming known, and it is not the same as involving relatives who have their own stake in the outcome.

That distinction matters, because a neutral professional can say things a well-meaning relative cannot, and has no interest in a particular result.

Myth 4
The counsellor will just tell me to adjust

This concern is raised most often by women, and it is not baseless. Marriage counselling in India has been criticised precisely for sometimes reinforcing unequal gender roles, treating compromise as the woman's responsibility and framing adjustment as the goal regardless of what is being adjusted to.

It is worth naming plainly: that is bad practice, not what the work is supposed to be. Competent couples therapy does not ask one partner to absorb more in order to keep the peace. It examines how responsibility, labour and decision-making are actually distributed, and whether that distribution is something both people genuinely agreed to.

You are entitled to assess this. If a counsellor consistently directs the adjusting toward one of you, or treats one partner's dissatisfaction as the problem to be managed, that is a reason to change clinician rather than to conclude counselling does not work.

Myth 5
There is no point if my partner will not come

A reluctant partner is one of the most common reasons couples never start, and it is not the barrier it appears to be.

You can work on a relationship on your own. Individual counselling focused on the relationship helps you understand your own part in a recurring dynamic and respond differently, which frequently changes the dynamic itself. It is also common for a hesitant partner to join later, once they see the process is not what they feared: no blame allocated, no verdict delivered.

Starting alone is a legitimate beginning, not a compromised version of the real thing.

What the evidence actually shows

Couples therapy is one of the better-studied areas in psychotherapy. Meta-analytic reviews of emotionally focused therapy, one of the main evidence-based approaches, report that roughly 70% of distressed couples recover and around 90% show significant improvement, with gains still holding at two-year follow-up in later studies. The Gottman Method, the other widely used approach, also shows measurable benefits in controlled trials for conflict resolution and emotional connection.

On timeframe, most couples complete somewhere between eight and twelve sessions. Many notice early shifts between the fourth and sixth, though rebuilding trust after a serious rupture generally takes several months of consistent work.

One important limit: couples counselling is not appropriate where there is abuse, coercion or fear of a partner. Joint sessions can make matters less safe in that situation. If that describes your relationship, seek individual support from a qualified professional first.

What actually happens when you book

Marriage counselling in Delhi follows a broadly similar shape wherever you go. Both partners usually attend the first session together, and some clinicians also hold a short individual conversation with each of you. The counsellor hears both perspectives, asks what has brought you now rather than a year ago, and agrees with you what the work should focus on.

It is an assessment, not a commitment to a long course of treatment. You are also assessing them, which is a reasonable thing to do openly.

On cost, published rates across Delhi generally start around ₹1,500 to ₹3,000 a session, with senior clinical psychologists charging more depending on experience and session format. These are market figures rather than ours, so confirm current fees with us directly when you book.

Talk to someone before you decide

You do not have to be certain about counselling, or about the relationship, to have a first conversation. See what couples therapy at eMbrace involves, or book a first session at our Delhi NCR centres and decide from there.
